subject: Regarding camera trap distance sampling analysis

messages.author: 0e4f91968e8a7f83
messages.subject: Regarding camera trap distance sampling analysis
parts:
Hello,

I am analysing a dataset of 220 randomly placed camera traps for estimating elephant density using CTDS. Out of the 220 camera traps elephants were captured in 52 traps. From this 39 trap-data could be used due to reasons such as, cameras disturbed by elephants on the first day of deployment or captures outside calibration distances. 

I have approximately 2600 elephant distance observations from the camera trap (after removing observations where the animal has reacted to the camera presence). The average camera trap effort was 40 days. I have not set any interval unlike Howe et al, 2017, since the cameras were set to capture continuous photos without any delay between the triggers.

I analysed the data following the online guide 'Analysis of camera trapping data' of Maxwell's duiker. 

I am getting a very high CV of 182 percent.

What could possibly be the reason for such a high CV? How shall I account for this?
I have not modelled density using CTDS before. 

Any suggestions would be much appreciated. 

Regards,

Sudip

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Regarding camera trap distance sampling analysis
parts:
Sudip

Thanks for your question. There could be several causes for the large uncertainty in you estimate of elephant density.

I would suggest you focus upon the variability in encounter rate; differences in detections between cameras.  You note most of your cameras had no detections; I suspect a few of your cameras may have had many detections, resulting in high between-camera variability in encounter rate. Examine your output focusing upon the reported encounter rates and more importantly CV of encounter rate.

I suspect you will find encounter rate is responsible for the majority of uncertainty in your density estimate. That is a common situation with camera trap data. There is considerable small scale heterogeneity in habitats which are manifested in high encounter rate variance.

How do you reduce encounter rate variability? I'm afraid this is an area of current research; I don't have an answer for you. Perhaps researchers who are active in this area and also read these questions might have a suggestion for you.
